title: Construction begins on giant underground neutrino experiment which involves Warwick academics
excerpt: A Warwick researcher is at the forefront of the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE), which aims to investigate some of the Universe’s biggest mysteries.
content:
Deep underground in South Dakota, construction is taking place on the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE), one of the world’s most ambitious particle physics experiments.

 Bringing together more than 1,500 researchers globally, DUNE aims to shed light on some of the Universe’s greatest mysteries.

Neutrinos are among the Universe's most abundant subatomic particles, but they rarely interact with matter, making them hard to detect. DUNE will use enormous detectors filled with liquid argon to record the tiny signals produced when neutrinos interact.

By comparing the particles detected at the two ends of this journey, scientists hope to shed light on some of the most fundamental questions in physics, including:

  • Why the Universe contains so much more matter than antimatter
  • How the early Universe evolved following the Big Bang
  • How neutrinos behave and change as they travel
  • What neutrinos can reveal about exploding stars, including supernovae.

A major milestone has now been reached, as teams from the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab), CERN and the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) begin construction of DUNE’s massive cryostats.

Professor Gary Barker from Warwick's Department of Physics is the Principal Investigator for the DUNE-UK collaboration. He commented: "The UK neutrino community is making a major contribution to DUNE, providing unique expertise to the international project across precision engineering, advanced software and physics analysis deliverables. This milestone is a key step towards our goal of having detectors installed underground and taking physics data."
 

The DUNE Reconstruction Software and Distributed Computing (RS&DC) project is led by physicists at the University of Warwick. It delivers the advanced software and computing infrastructure that will ultimately help to turn data collected by the DUNE detectors into world-leading physics results.

DUNE is planned for completion by 2029, with the detector apparatus scheduled to be finished in 2030.
